questions.question: Which of the reagents will dehydrate an alcohol to an alkene?
questions.answer: Concentrated sulfuric acid is a dehydrating agent that removes water from an alcohol (elimination) to form an alkene (D). Acidified permanganate oxidises alcohols and bromine water reacts with alkenes; dilute acid contains too much water.

questions.question: Which compound is a functional group isomer of pentan-2-one?
questions.answer: Pentan-2-one is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ (a ketone). A functional group isomer has the same formula but a different functional group: pentanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, an aldehyde (B). A and D are the ketone pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one (not functional group isomers), and C is an ester with a different formula.

questions.question: The structure of a compound is shown. What is the IUPAC preferred name for this compound?
questions.answer: The structure is a five-carbon chain: $\text{CHF}_2-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$. The principal functional group (OH) gets the lowest number, so number from the $\text{CH}_3$ end: OH on C2, Cl on C4, two F on C5. Substituents are listed alphabetically: 4-chloro-5,5-difluoropentan-2-ol (D).

questions.question: A student was carrying out an experiment to isolate the components of a solution containing iodide, carbonate, and sulfate ions using precipitation reactions. Which of the following reagents would be invalid for this procedure?
questions.answer: Sulfuric acid would react with carbonate ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}+2\text{H}^+\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$), destroying it, and would add extra sulfate ions that would interfere with the sulfate in the sample (A). The others are suitable: nitric acid can be used to dissolve carbonate precipitates, silver nitrate precipitates the halide, and magnesium nitrate precipitates carbonate.

questions.question: The diagram shows the key components in a UV-Visible spectrophotometer. When the instrument is operated to measure the absorbance of a sample, the intensity of light is recorded at two different locations. Which pair of measurements is subtracted to find the light absorption?
questions.answer: Absorbance depends on the intensity of light entering the sample (Y, after the monochromator's exit slit) compared with the intensity leaving the sample (Z, at the detector). The light absorbed is $Y-Z$ (C).

questions.question: Which molecule has a linear shape?
questions.answer: Ethyne ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$) has a triple bond, so each carbon has two regions of electron density and a bond angle of $180^\circ$ (linear) (A). Ethene is planar ($120^\circ$); ethane and methane are tetrahedral ($109.5^\circ$ at each carbon).

questions.question: The graph shows a conductivity titration graph. Which type of acid-base titration is illustrated with the shape of this graph?
questions.answer: The conductance falls as the highly conducting $\text{H}^+$ is neutralised, then levels off after the equivalence point because the excess weak base is only slightly ionised and adds few ions (B). A strong base would cause a sharp increase after the equivalence point (as in strong acid vs strong base, which shows a V-shape). A weak acid starts with low conductance.

questions.question: Which of the following would turn pink litmus blue?
questions.answer: Pink (acidic) litmus turns blue in a basic solution. Methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, is an amine, a weak base that accepts a proton from water, forming $\text{OH}^-$ (D). The alkane, alcohol and ester are neutral.

questions.question: Which of the following salt solutions would give a blue grey flame colour?
questions.answer: Lead ions give a blue-grey (pale blue-white) flame (A). Copper gives green/blue-green, barium gives pale green and calcium gives orange-red.

questions.question: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) is introduced into a sealed vessel and left to reach equilibrium according to $\text{CO}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)$. Which of the following changes to the system is consistent with the shift to the equilibrium?
questions.answer: Adding gaseous $\text{CO}_2$ increases the concentration of the product, so the system shifts left (towards the solid) to partly counteract the change (C). Doubling the volume would shift right (the pressure of gas falls), raising the temperature favours the endothermic sublimation (shifts right), and adding more of a pure solid does not change the position of equilibrium.
options: Doubling of reaction volume: system shifts left
Increase of reaction temperature: no change
Addition of more gaseous $\text{CO}_2$: system shifts left
Addition of more dry ice: system shifts right

questions.question: Two solutions of the same concentration, Y and Z, had pH measurements of 2.00 and 4.00 respectively. Which statement about solutions Y and Z is correct?
questions.answer: $[\text{H}^+]_Y=10^{-2}$ M and $[\text{H}^+]_Z=10^{-4}$ M, so Y has 100 times the $[\text{H}^+]$ of Z (D). Correspondingly $[\text{OH}^-]$ in Z is 100 times that in Y.
options: The concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Z is 10 times greater than the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Y.
The concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Z is two times greater than the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Y.
The concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Y is two times greater than the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Z.
The concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Y is 100 times greater than the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Z.

questions.question: Glycine is an amino acid that can undergo condensation polymerisation. What is the molar mass of the polymer formed from 1000 glycine monomer units?
questions.answer: Glycine, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$, has $M=75.07\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Joining 1000 units releases 999 molecules of water: $M=1000\times75.07-999\times18.016=7.507\times10^4-1.800\times10^4=5.7\times10^4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ (C).

questions.question: A student has three dropper bottles containing: A, sodium carbonate, 0.0001 M; B, silver sulfate, 0.001 M; C, lead chloride, 0.0005 M. The student places a plastic sheet on a black bench and combines a drop from two different dropper bottles (A+B, A+C and B+C). How many of the three combinations would show ‘No visible reaction’?
questions.answer: In each case a precipitate forms: A+B gives silver carbonate ($\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$, $K_{sp}\approx8\times10^{-12}$; after mixing $Q\approx(1\times10^{-3})^2(5\times10^{-5})=5\times10^{-11}>K_{sp}$), A+C gives lead carbonate ($\text{PbCO}_3$) and B+C gives silver chloride ($\text{AgCl}$, and lead sulfate). So no combination is without a visible reaction: 0 (A).

questions.question: The gas-phase reaction $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$ has $K=46$. 0.22 mol of hydrogen, 0.63 mol of iodine and 2.40 mol of hydrogen iodide were added to a 110 L container. Which of the following correctly identifies the relationship between $Q$ and $K$ and the equilibrium shift?
questions.answer: Since the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, the volume cancels: $Q=\dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}=\dfrac{2.40^2}{0.22\times0.63}=41.6$. $Q<K=46$, so the reaction shifts right to form more product (B).

questions.question: An experiment measures the temperature change for a heat of combustion reaction. 100.0 mL of water at 308 K was heated by the burning of 1.05 g of ethanol in the spirit burner. Only 45.0% of the energy produced was used to heat the water. The molar heat of combustion of ethanol is $-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. What is the final temperature of the water?
questions.answer: $n(\text{ethanol})=\dfrac{1.05}{46.068}=0.02279$ mol; energy $=0.02279\times1367=31.2$ kJ; energy to the water $=0.450\times31.2=14.0$ kJ. $\Delta T=\dfrac{14.0\times10^3}{100.0\times4.18}=33.6$ K. The initial temperature is $308\ \text{K}=34.85^\circ\text{C}$, so the final temperature is $34.85+33.6\approx68.5^\circ\text{C}$ (C).

questions.question: A molecule of 2-chlorobutanal is shown, with an arrow pointing to the hydrogen on carbon 2 (the carbon bonded to the chlorine). Which of the following shows the splitting pattern observed for the labelled environment in the proton NMR spectrum for this molecule?
questions.answer: The labelled hydrogen is on C2, which is bonded to C1 (the aldehyde carbon, 1 H) and C3 ($\text{CH}_2$, 2 H). It has $1+2=3$ neighbouring hydrogens, so by the $n+1$ rule it splits into a quartet (C).

questions.question: An investigation using gravimetric analysis was carried out to determine the identity of an anion in a solution. Adding 0.04 mol of silver ions resulted in the production of 5.52 g of precipitate. Which of the following is a possible identity for the anion?
questions.answer: Calculate the molar mass of the precipitate for each option: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$: $n=0.02$ mol, $m=0.02\times275.75=5.51$ g (matches); AgBr: $0.04\times187.77=7.51$ g; AgI: $0.04\times234.77=9.39$ g; $\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$: $\dfrac{0.04}{3}\times418.58=5.58$ g. 5.52 g is closest to the carbonate (A).

questions.question: An organic molecule with the chemical formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$ gives the mass spectrum shown (molecular ion at $m/z$ 58, base peak at $m/z$ 43). Which of the following would give the mass spectrum shown?
questions.answer: The base peak at $m/z$ 43 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ ($12\times2+3+16=43$), formed by losing a methyl group from propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ (B). Propanal would fragment mainly to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ ($m/z$ 29) and $\text{CHO}^+$ ($m/z$ 29), and the enols are unstable.

questions.question: 25.0 mL of a $1.00\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution in a conical flask is titrated against $1.00\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid solution. What volume of hydrochloric acid must be added to achieve a pH of 1 in the mixture?
questions.answer: pH 1 means $[\text{H}^+]=0.10$ M. With $V$ mL of acid added, excess $\text{H}^+=\dfrac{V-25.0}{V+25.0}\times1.00=0.10$, so $V-25.0=0.10V+2.5$ and $V=30.6$ mL. The closest option is 30.0 mL (C).

questions.question: An investigation determined the amount of manganese in a sample of fertiliser. 5.67 g of the fertiliser was dissolved and treated to perform $\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)+4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+8\text{H}^+(aq)+5e^-$. The resulting permanganate solution was transferred to a 100 mL volumetric flask and filled to the mark. A sample gave an absorbance of 0.45 in a colorimeter, and was compared with the calibration curve provided. What is the percentage mass of manganese ions in the fertiliser sample?
questions.answer: From the calibration curve, an absorbance of 0.45 corresponds to $[\text{MnO}_4^-]\approx2.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. $n=2.25\times10^{-4}\times0.100=2.25\times10^{-5}$ mol $=n(\text{Mn}^{2+})$. $m=2.25\times10^{-5}\times54.94=1.24\times10^{-3}$ g, so $\%=\dfrac{1.24\times10^{-3}}{5.67}\times100=0.022\%\approx0.02\%$ (A).

questions.question: But-2-ene undergoes an addition reaction with water. Give the name and structural formula of the product of this reaction.
questions.answer: Water adds across the double bond: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The product is butan-2-ol: a four-carbon chain with an $-\text{OH}$ group on carbon 2.

questions.question: A chemist has proposed the integration of an electrochemical cell into the well-established Haber-Bosch process used for the industrial synthesis of ammonia. This would replace the conventional temperature and pressure system, which is driven by the combustion of fossil fuels. An overview of the design is presented in the diagram (a PCMR cell fed with methane/biogas and steam, producing $\text{CO}_2$/$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and ammonia, and a PCFC cell fed with air that generates electricity and recycles $\text{N}_2$/$\text{H}_2$). Using the diagram, explain TWO advantages associated with the use of electrochemical cells in this process.
questions.answer:
Advantage 1: the electrochemical cells allow the use of renewable energy (solar and wind electricity) and renewable reagents (biogas) in place of fossil fuels. This avoids the large pollution (greenhouse gas emissions) from burning fossil fuels for high temperature and pressure and conserves a finite resource.

Advantage 2: the two cells allow recycling of chemicals and electricity. Unreacted $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ are returned to the PCMR cell, and the PCFC cell generates electricity that is used to power the PCMR cell. This reduces the costs of reagents and of external electrical energy, and improves the efficiency (yield) of the process.

questions.question: Determine how many grams of calcium sulfate will dissolve in 100.0 mL of a $0.0020\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution of sodium sulfate. ($K_{sp}(\text{CaSO}_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$)

Consider the reaction at equilibrium: $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{NO}_3(g)+\text{NO}_2(g)$. Le Chatelier's principle and collision theory can both be used to understand the behaviour of equilibrium systems. Show how both of these can be used to explain the change that occurs to the system when some $\text{NO}_3(g)$ is removed.
questions.answer:
Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the system shifts to partially counteract the change. $\text{NO}_3(g)$, a product, is removed, so the position shifts to the right to form more $\text{NO}_3$ until a new equilibrium is reached.

Collision theory: reaction rates depend on the number of successful collisions per second. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal. When some $\text{NO}_3$ is removed, there are fewer $\text{NO}_3$ molecules to collide with $\text{NO}_2$, so the rate of the reverse reaction decreases immediately, while the forward rate is initially unchanged. The forward rate is therefore greater than the reverse rate, and there is a net shift right. As this occurs, $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]$ falls, so the forward rate decreases, and $[\text{NO}_3]$ rises, so the reverse rate increases, until the two rates are again equal and a new equilibrium is established.

questions.question: An analytical chemist added 2.56 g of barium hydroxide to 0.250 L of a $0.200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution of nitric acid in a 400 mL beaker. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. Assume the total volume remains unchanged.
Explain how nitric acid meets the criteria for the Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry models of acids. Use equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
An Arrhenius acid is a substance that ionises in water to produce hydrogen (hydronium) ions: $\text{HNO}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{NO}_3^-(aq)$. Nitric acid is a strong acid, so it ionises completely (one-way arrow).

A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor. $\text{HNO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{NO}_3^-(aq)$. Here $\text{HNO}_3$ (acid) donates a proton to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (base), forming the conjugate acid $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and the conjugate base $\text{NO}_3^-$.

questions.question: Ethanol is produced through fermentation of glucose solution. The reaction is carried out in a school laboratory, and the volume of carbon dioxide generated is measured under standard laboratory conditions (25 °C and 100 kPa). Hours / total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ (mL): 0 / 0; 20 / 500; 40 / 760; 60 / 900; 80 / 960; 100 / 960; 120 / 960. Describe how the results would be plotted as a graph, including the line of best fit, and state the volume of $\text{CO}_2$ produced at 30 hours from your graph.
questions.answer: Plot time (hours) on the horizontal axis (0 to 120, scale 20 h per division) and total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ (mL) on the vertical axis (0 to 1000, with units), label both axes, plot the seven points accurately, and draw a smooth curve of best fit (not straight lines joining the points). The curve rises steeply from the origin, becomes less steep, and levels off at 960 mL from 80 hours (see the graph). At 30 hours the curve reads about 640 mL (accept 620–660 mL).

questions.question: Ethanol is produced through fermentation of glucose solution, with the total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ produced measured over time: 0 h: 0 mL; 20 h: 500 mL; 40 h: 760 mL; 60 h: 900 mL; 80 h: 960 mL; 100 h: 960 mL; 120 h: 960 mL. Explain the shape of the graph of volume against time.
questions.answer: The volume of $\text{CO}_2$ increases until it reaches a maximum of 960 mL and then plateaus, because all of the glucose has been used up (or the yeast has been killed by the concentration of ethanol), so no more $\text{CO}_2$ is produced. The graph is a curve, not a straight line, because the rate of reaction decreases as the reactants are used up: there are fewer reactant particles and so fewer successful collisions per second. The curve is steep at the start, when the concentration of glucose is highest, and gradually becomes shallower as the rate decreases.

questions.question: In the fermentation of glucose, a total of 960 mL of $\text{CO}_2$ gas was collected under standard laboratory conditions (25 °C and 100 kPa; molar volume 24.79 L mol$^{-1}$). Calculate the mass of ethanol produced in this reaction. Include a relevant equation in your answer.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{CO}_2(g)+2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)$. $n(\text{CO}_2)=\dfrac{0.960}{24.79}=0.03872$ mol. $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=n(\text{CO}_2)=0.03872$ mol. $m=0.03872\times46.07=1.78$ g.

questions.question: 25.00 mL of a straight chain gaseous hydrocarbon was reacted with 200.0 mL of oxygen at 25 °C. On cooling to 25 °C, the residual mixture of gases had a volume of 137.5 mL. This was shaken with potassium hydroxide solution to remove the carbon dioxide, dropping the final gas volume to 37.50 mL, consisting of oxygen only. Show your relevant working to identify the hydrocarbon.
questions.answer: $V(\text{CO}_2)=137.5-37.5=100.0$ mL. $V(\text{O}_2\text{ used})=200.0-37.5=162.5$ mL. By Gay-Lussac's law, volumes of gases at the same conditions are in the ratio of moles, so $\text{C}_x\text{H}_y:\text{O}_2:\text{CO}_2=25:162.5:100=1:6.5:4$. So $x=4$ and the equation is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}+6.5\text{O}_2\rightarrow4\text{CO}_2+5\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (oxygen balance: $2\times4+y/2=13$, so $y=10$). The hydrocarbon is butane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$.

questions.question: Give the structural formula of 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.
questions.answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-CO-CH(CH}_3)_2$: a five-carbon chain with a carbonyl group ($\text{C=O}$) on carbon 3 and a methyl group on each of carbons 2 and 4.

questions.question: Outline the information that could be obtained about 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one using infrared spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Infrared spectroscopy gives information on the functional groups present. It would show a strong peak for the $\text{C=O}$ stretch at about $1680$–$1750\ \text{cm}^{-1}$, identifying a ketone (and no broad O–H peak).

questions.question: Describe the information that could be obtained about 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one using carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Carbon-13 NMR shows the number of different carbon environments and the types of carbon. A signal at about $190$–$220$ ppm would identify the carbonyl carbon of a ketone. It also shows the symmetry in the molecule: although the molecule has 7 carbon atoms, there would be only 3 signals (the carbonyl carbon, the two equivalent CH carbons, and the four equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ carbons).

questions.question: The pH in swimming pools is maintained between 7.2 and 7.8, commonly by adding sodium hydrogen carbonate at regular intervals. Which physical property of solid sodium hydrogen carbonate makes it suitable for use in swimming pool water?
questions.answer: It is highly soluble in water.

questions.question: Define the role of a buffer in an aqueous environment.
questions.answer: A buffer is a soluble chemical system (usually a weak acid and its conjugate base) that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, so that the solution stays within a narrow pH range.

questions.question: Justify the use of sodium hydrogen carbonate as a suitable buffer in swimming pools. Provide relevant chemical equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
Sodium hydrogen carbonate dissolves to give the hydrogen carbonate ion, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, which is amphiprotic: it can act as a weak acid or a weak base (and sits in equilibrium with carbonate and carbonic acid), so it can neutralise small additions of acid or base and keep the pH constant (in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle).

When acid is added: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(aq)$.

When base is added: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$.

These reactions maintain the pH within the range 7.2–7.8, minimising skin and eye irritation for swimmers.

questions.question: A $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonium chloride solution has a pH of 4.60. What is the $K_a$ of this weak acid ($\text{NH}_4^+$)?
questions.answer: $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=10^{-4.60}=2.51\times10^{-5}$ M. ICE: initial $[\text{NH}_4^+]=0.100$, $[\text{NH}_3]=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=0$; change $-s,+s,+s$ with $s=2.51\times10^{-5}$; equilibrium $[\text{NH}_4^+]=0.100-2.51\times10^{-5}\approx0.100$, $[\text{NH}_3]=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=2.51\times10^{-5}$. $K_a=\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{NH}_4^+]}=\dfrac{(2.51\times10^{-5})^2}{0.100}=6.3\times10^{-9}$.

questions.question: A $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonium chloride solution has a pH of 4.60. What is the percent ionisation of the acid ($\text{NH}_4^+$)?
questions.answer: $\%\text{ionisation}=\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]}{[\text{NH}_4^+]_{initial}}\times100=\dfrac{2.51\times10^{-5}}{0.100}\times100=0.0251\%$.

questions.question: The $K_a$ of the ammonium ion is $6.3\times10^{-9}$. Calculate its $pK_a$.

A primary straight chained alcohol, a carboxylic acid and an ester made with methanol are colourless liquids with molar masses of $88\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Identify the compounds and explain the results of physical and chemical tests that could be performed to distinguish between the three liquids.
questions.answer:
The compounds: the alcohol is pentan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{OH}$ ($M=88.15$); the carboxylic acid is butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($M=88.11$); the ester made with methanol is methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$ ($M=88.11$).

Physical tests: Boiling points. Methyl propanoate has the lowest, because it has no O–H group, so only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act between molecules. Pentan-1-ol is higher as it has dispersion forces and hydrogen bonding. Butanoic acid has the highest because its molecules form more extensive (stronger) hydrogen bonding, needing the most energy to overcome. (Observed boiling points: methyl propanoate about $80^\circ\text{C}$, pentan-1-ol about $138^\circ\text{C}$, butanoic acid about $164^\circ\text{C}$.) Solubility in water: butanoic acid is completely miscible (polar, hydrogen bonds with water); pentan-1-ol is only slightly soluble, as the hydroxyl group hydrogen bonds with water but the longer non-polar chain limits solubility; the ester is insoluble and forms a layer above the water (and has a fruity smell).

Chemical tests: add acidified permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$): the primary alcohol is oxidised (to a carboxylic acid), decolourising the purple permanganate, while the acid and ester do not react. Add sodium carbonate or hydrogen carbonate solution: only the carboxylic acid reacts, producing bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$ gas, while the alcohol and ester do not.

questions.question: Solutions 1–6 were prepared to produce a standard curve for $\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}$, with volumes of $0.0010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ of 0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0 mL, 5.0 mL of $4.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$ in each, and 5.0, 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0 and 0 mL of water respectively. Explain the purpose of the water in solutions 1–5.
questions.answer: The water makes the total volume of each of the six solutions 10.0 mL. This means the $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ concentration increases in regular amounts across the solutions, while the concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ stays identical in each solution (2.0 M), so that the concentration of the complex ion depends only on the volume of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ added, and the absorbance readings can be validly compared.

questions.question: The complex ion forms in $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)+6\text{NH}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}(aq)$. A standard curve of absorbance against $[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]$ is provided (absorbance 0, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16 and 0.20 at concentrations $0$ to $5\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ in steps of $1\times10^{-4}$). The student made a new solution using 1.0 mL of $0.0070\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)$, 1.0 mL of $0.40\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$ and 8.0 mL of water. An absorbance of 0.17 was recorded. Calculate the value of $K_{eq}$ for the complexation reaction.
questions.answer: Dilution (total volume 10.0 mL): initial $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]=0.0070\times\dfrac{1}{10}=7.0\times10^{-4}$ M and $[\text{NH}_3]=0.40\times\dfrac{1}{10}=0.040$ M. From the standard curve, an absorbance of 0.17 corresponds to $[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]=4.25\times10^{-4}$ M (accept 4.2–4.3 $\times10^{-4}$). ICE: $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]=7.0\times10^{-4}-4.25\times10^{-4}=2.75\times10^{-4}$ M; $[\text{NH}_3]=0.040-6(4.25\times10^{-4})=0.0375$ M. $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^6}=\dfrac{4.25\times10^{-4}}{(2.75\times10^{-4})(0.0375)^6}=5.6\times10^{8}$.

questions.question: For the complexation reaction $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)+6\text{NH}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}(aq)$ with $K_{eq}\gg1$: in making the standard curve, the student treated the reaction as having gone to completion with $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ as the limiting reagent (ammonia concentration 2.0 M, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ at most $5\times10^{-4}$ M). When determining the unknown $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ in the later solution (ammonia only 0.040 M, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ $7\times10^{-4}$ M), the system was treated as an equilibrium. Account for the two different treatments.
questions.answer: $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{complex}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^6}$, so $\dfrac{[\text{complex}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}=K_{eq}[\text{NH}_3]^6$. In the standard curve solutions the ammonia concentration was very high (at least 1.997 M, more than 4000 times that of nickel), so $[\text{NH}_3]^6$ is large, the ratio $[\text{complex}]/[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$ is huge, and the equilibrium lies so far to the right that essentially all of the $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is complexed, so assuming completion is reasonable. In the second experiment the ammonia concentration was much lower (0.040 M, only about 57 times the nickel concentration), and since it is less than 1 M, $[\text{NH}_3]^6$ is tiny ($\approx2.8\times10^{-9}$ here, and the ratio is about 1.5, not $\gg1$), so the position of equilibrium is not as far right and not all of the nickel was complexed. An equilibrium (ICE table) treatment was therefore needed.

questions.question: An investigation used a series of precipitation reactions to determine the concentration of magnesium, silver and copper ions in a sample solution. A 25.0 mL aliquot was reacted with hydrochloric acid until no more precipitate formed; the precipitate was filtered and dried to a mass of 1.36 g. The filtrate was neutralised with dilute ammonia, and sodium hydroxide was added until no more precipitate formed; the mixture of blue and white precipitates, filtered and dried, had a mass of 2.40 g. In a separate experiment, a 20.0 mL aliquot of the sample was titrated with $0.427\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium carbonate; a pale yellow silver precipitate formed first, then a blue copper precipitate, then a white magnesium precipitate. The titre volume was recorded once the white precipitate began to form: 41.10, 39.75, 39.85 and 39.80 mL. Calculate the concentrations of magnesium, silver and copper ions in the original sample solution. Include a relevant chemical equation for each precipitation reaction.
questions.answer:
Silver (HCl step): $\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{AgCl}(s)$. $n(\text{AgCl})=\dfrac{1.36}{143.35}=9.49\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{Ag}^+)$; $[\text{Ag}^+]=\dfrac{9.49\times10^{-3}}{0.0250}=0.380\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Copper (carbonate titration; discard the outlier 41.10 mL): average titre $=\dfrac{39.75+39.85+39.80}{3}=39.80$ mL. $2\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(s)$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{CuCO}_3(s)$. $n(\text{CO}_3^{2-})=0.427\times0.03980=0.01700$ mol. In the 20.0 mL aliquot, $n(\text{Ag}^+)=0.380\times0.0200=7.59\times10^{-3}$ mol, which uses $\dfrac{7.59\times10^{-3}}{2}=3.80\times10^{-3}$ mol of carbonate. $n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=0.01700-0.00380=0.01320$ mol, so $[\text{Cu}^{2+}]=\dfrac{0.01320}{0.0200}=0.660\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Magnesium (hydroxide precipitate, 25.0 mL aliquot): $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$. $n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=0.660\times0.0250=0.0165$ mol, $m(\text{Cu(OH)}_2)=0.0165\times97.57=1.61$ g. $m(\text{Mg(OH)}_2)=2.40-1.61=0.79$ g, $n=\dfrac{0.79}{58.33}=0.0135$ mol $=n(\text{Mg}^{2+})$. $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]=\dfrac{0.0135}{0.0250}=0.54\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

questions.question: The following information was obtained from the analysis of an unknown organic compound. Chemical reactivity: $\text{NaHCO}_3(aq)$ gave bubbling; $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4(aq)$ stayed a dark magenta solution; $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ gave a colourless solution. Mass spectrum: molecular ion at $m/z$ 114, base peak at $m/z$ 69, other peaks at about 43, 45, 71, 97 and 99. Proton NMR: singlet, 1 H, about 11 ppm; triplet, 1 H, about 7.2 ppm; doublet, 1 H, about 6.0 ppm; octet, 1 H, about 2.7 ppm; doublet, 6 H, about 1.2 ppm. Give the structural formula for the unknown compound that is consistent with all the information provided. Justify your structure with reference to the relevant information from each source of data.
questions.answer:
The compound is 4-methylpent-2-enoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-CH=CH-COOH}$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$).

Chemical reactivity: bubbles with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ show an acid ($\text{CO}_2$ is released), so there is a carboxylic acid group. Bromine water is decolourised by an addition reaction, showing a $\text{C=C}$ double bond is present. (The school's solution reads the unchanged magenta colour of acidified permanganate as showing no alcohol or aldehyde is present; note that an alkene would normally also decolourise permanganate, so this observation is not consistent with an alkene, and the bromine test is the evidence for the double bond.)

Mass spectrum: the molecular ion at $m/z=114$ gives the molar mass. $\text{COOH}$ has mass 45, leaving 69 for the carbon chain. The 10 hydrogens in the NMR, less 1 for the acid group, leave 9 H on the chain, and the chain is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9$ ($60+9=69$), which includes the double bond. The base peak at 69 is $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH=CH}]^+$ (loss of $\text{COOH}$); 71 is $[\text{CH=CHCOOH}]^+$; 97 is loss of OH ($[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH=CHCO}]^+$); 99 is loss of $\text{CH}_3$; 43 is $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}]^+$; and 45 is $[\text{COOH}]^+$.

Proton NMR: the 1 H singlet at about 11 ppm is the carboxylic acid proton, with no neighbouring hydrogens. The 6 H doublet at about 1.2 ppm is two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups, each next to one H (the CH). That CH is the 1 H octet at about 2.7 ppm (split by 6 H from the two methyls plus 1 H from the alkene CH, so $n+1=8$). The alkene H next to it is the signal at about 7.2 ppm (1 H) and the other alkene H (next to COOH) is at about 6.0 ppm (1 H, doublet because it is next to only one H). This gives the fragments $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-}$, $-\text{CH=CH-}$ and $-\text{COOH}$ joined in order.

questions.question: Discuss the effects of enthalpy and entropy in the reaction between octane and oxygen in a flame.
questions.answer:
The reaction is $2\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}(l)+25\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow16\text{CO}_2(g)+18\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$ (the water is a gas in the flame, as the temperature is above $100^\circ\text{C}$).

Enthalpy: combustion is highly exothermic ($\Delta H<0$): the stronger bonds formed in the products release more energy than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants, and the energy is released as heat (and light), which favours the reaction.

Entropy: there are 25 mol of gas in the reactants (plus liquid octane) and 34 mol of gas in the products, so the number of gas particles increases, the dispersal of matter and energy increases and $\Delta S>0$, which also favours the reaction.

$\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$: with $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S>0$, $\Delta G$ is negative at all temperatures, so the reaction is spontaneous. (A spark or flame is needed only to provide the activation energy to start the reaction, not because it is non-spontaneous.)
